focus: Section 3.5 Positional Encoding. Explain the sinusoidal positional encodings: each dimension is a sinusoid whose wavelength grows geometrically with the dimension index. Let the learner change the model dimension d_model, the position and the dimension index. Show the encoding vector for a position, the heatmap of positions x dimensions, and the wavelengths. Guide the learner through low versus high dimensions (fast versus slow oscillation) and through the dot product between encodings of nearby versus distant positions. Check that every value lies in [-1, 1] and that sin^2 + cos^2 = 1 for each frequency pair.
audience: engineering undergraduate who has seen sine waves and vectors
excerpt: 3.5 Positional Encoding (paraphrased). Since our model contains no recurrence and no convolution, in order for the model to make use of the order of the sequence, we must inject some information about the relative or absolute position of the tokens in the sequence. To this end, we add positional encodings to the input embeddings at the bottoms of the encoder and decoder stacks. The positional encodings have the same dimension d_model as the embeddings, so that the two can be summed. In this work, we use sine and cosine functions of different frequencies: PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos / 10000^(2i/d_model)), PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(pos / 10000^(2i/d_model)), where pos is the position and i is the dimension. That is, each dimension of the positional encoding corresponds to a sinusoid. The wavelengths form a geometric progression from 2*pi to 10000*2*pi. We chose this function because we hypothesized it would allow the model to easily learn to attend by relative positions, since for any fixed offset k, PE(pos+k) can be represented as a linear function of PE(pos).
